Where capacity declined, ask whether the cost was temporary and recovered, or cumulative and unresolved. Note whose unseen labor made the quarter possible.

Hidden support or sacrifice: ______________________________

Repair or redesign required: ______________________________

Do not interpret another person's continued help as unlimited consent. Reopen the support conversation.

F. Review the Quality of Learning

Count neither failures nor experiments alone. Ask whether the model changed.

Which assumption was revised? ____________________________

Which process changed because of a failure or near miss? ___

Which mistake repeated? __________________________________

Which success may have depended on luck? _________________

What did you stop doing because evidence was clear? _______

If nothing changed despite repeated unfavorable results, persistence has become repetition.

G. Review Decision Quality

Select two decisions: one that produced a good outcome and one that produced a bad outcome. Evaluate the process without allowing the outcome to decide the grade.

Was the objective clear? Was relevant evidence sought? Were alternatives considered? Were affected people included? Was exposure proportionate? Were boundaries respected? Was uncertainty recorded? Did the decision include a review point?

Good-outcome decision, process strengths and weaknesses: ___

Bad-outcome decision, process strengths and weaknesses: ____

Name one decision habit to preserve and one to change.

Preserve: _______________________________________________

Change: _________________________________________________

H. Choose the Next Direction

Make the strongest case for continue, adjust, pause, and stop in no more than four sentences each. Then choose.

Direction for the next period: ____________________________

Reason: _________________________________________________

Most important uncertainty: ______________________________

Maximum exposure: _______________________________________

Turnaround trigger: ______________________________________

Next review: ____________________________________________

I. Write the Ninety-Day Contract

During the next period, I will pursue __________________ by __________________. I will protect __________________, seek evidence about __________________, and involve __________________. I will not increase exposure beyond __________________ without review. I will reconsider the direction if __________________ occurs. The next formal decision will be made on __________________.

Sign and date the contract. Send the parts that affect other people to them. A private plan cannot govern a shared burden.

Workbook 15: Shared Goals and Collective Decisions

Some commitments cannot be evaluated by one person alone. Partnerships, families, teams, communities, and organizations contain multiple values, unequal power, distributed costs, and overlapping rights.

Shared persistence is not unanimity. It is a process that makes decision rights, evidence, burden, and dissent visible.

A. Define What Is Actually Shared

Two people can use the same goal language while imagining different outcomes.

For example, “grow the business” may mean higher revenue to one partner, a saleable asset to another, and stable employment to the team. “Support the move” may mean emotional encouragement to one spouse and agreement to leave a career to the other.

Ask each participant to complete separately:

The shared goal is: ______________________________________

Success would look like: _________________________________

The reason it matters is: ________________________________

The cost I expect to carry is: ____________________________

The cost I am not willing or able to carry is: _____________

The decision I believe is mine, yours, or shared is: ________

Compare answers without correcting them immediately. The differences are the beginning of the real decision.

B. Map Decision Rights

For each major choice, identify who:

Proposes

Provides expertise

Must consent

Decides

Executes

Bears consequence

Can call a safety or ethics stop

Authority should not be inferred only from who speaks most confidently or supplies money. A funder may have contractual rights without owning another person's body or identity. A leader may decide strategy while professionals retain safety duties. A household member affected by debt or relocation may have legitimate consent rights.

Decision rights should be explicit before conflict. If they cannot be agreed, that disagreement is itself a constraint on the goal.

C. Audit Burden Distribution

List visible and invisible work: planning, earning, caregiving, emotional regulation, scheduling, transportation, administration, conflict repair, and risk.

Person or group: _________________________________________

Visible contribution: ____________________________________

Invisible contribution: __________________________________

Risk carried: ____________________________________________

Recognition or benefit received: __________________________

Choice available to them: ________________________________

Persistence becomes exploitative when one person's meaningful goal requires another person's unchosen depletion. Not every burden can be equal, but it should be visible, discussed, and bounded.

Ask: “Whose resilience is this plan quietly spending?”

D. Create a Dissent Channel

Groups often say dissent is welcome while rewarding only enthusiasm. Create a route that does not depend on public confrontation.

Named reviewer or ombudsperson: __________________________

Private reporting method: ________________________________

Response timeframe: _____________________________________

Protection against retaliation: ___________________________

Criteria for escalating the concern: ______________________

In a small partnership or family, the channel may be a scheduled conversation with a counselor, adviser, or trusted mediator. In high-stakes institutional settings, use formal safety, legal, human-resources, regulatory, or professional processes as appropriate.

Do not use a group decision framework to manage abuse or coercion as if it were an ordinary disagreement. Safety and specialized support come first.

E. Run the Shared Evidence Review

Before the meeting, distribute the evidence in a form participants can examine. Separate records from the interpretation preferred by leadership.

During the review, ask:

What did we predict?

What happened?

Who experienced a cost not represented in the dashboard?

Which evidence is missing because people were afraid, excluded, or unable to report it?

What assumption changed?

What are we continuing mainly because of identity, prestige, or past cost?

What do those closest to the consequence see that distant decision-makers do not?

Record minority views. A dissenting forecast should not disappear because the majority chooses another route. At the next review, compare outcomes with both forecasts.

F. Set Collective Turnaround Rules

Write thresholds for money, time, quality, safety, ethics, and capacity. Name who can freeze additional exposure and who conducts the review.

Trigger: ________________________________________________

Immediate action: ________________________________________

Stop authority: __________________________________________

Review participants: _____________________________________

Data required: ___________________________________________

Maximum additional exposure after review: ________________

Teams should not require the least powerful person to become heroic in order for the rule to function.

G. Decide When People Prefer Different Directions

Begin by locating the disagreement.

Do participants disagree about facts, values, risk tolerance, obligations, timing, or the distribution of cost? Each type requires a different response.

Facts: Seek better evidence or a bounded test.

Values: Identify what cannot be traded and whether coexistence is possible.

Risk: Clarify who bears downside and who has consent rights.

Obligations: Review contracts, duties, and promises with appropriate guidance.

Timing: Consider a defined pause or staged commitment.

Distribution: Redesign burden, benefit, authority, or exit options.

If disagreement remains, use the decision-rights map. A shared goal may need to become two separate goals. A partner may decline additional investment while allowing the other to proceed without shared resources. A team member may leave the project. An institution may decide within its authority while remaining accountable for impact.

Compromise is not automatically fair. Splitting the difference on a safety threshold can be irresponsible. Nor is complete agreement always possible. The process should preserve dignity, consent, and clear responsibility even when preferences diverge.

H. Close a Shared Commitment

Endings require coordination.

List what must be communicated, delivered, paid, transferred, archived, returned, repaired, or grieved. Name an owner and deadline for each task.

Closing task: ____________________________________________

Owner: __________________________________________________

Affected person: _________________________________________

Deadline: _______________________________________________

Evidence of completion: __________________________________

Hold a closing review. Ask what the group is proud of, what harm requires acknowledgment, what knowledge should be stored, and what relationships should continue outside the project.

Do not force a positive lesson. Some endings are losses. The purpose of the review is accuracy and responsible transfer.

I. The Collective Commitment Statement

We are choosing to continue / adjust / pause / stop __________________ because the strongest shared evidence shows __________________. This decision protects __________________ and costs __________________. Decision authority rests with __________________, while __________________ retains the right to __________________. We will complete __________________, monitor __________________, and review on __________________. Dissenting concerns that remain are __________________.

Have the appropriate decision-makers and affected parties confirm the parts that govern them. The statement will not remove conflict. It will prevent conflict from being hidden beneath a slogan about commitment.

Workbook 16: The Forty-Eight-Hour Reset

Use this reset when emotion is high, the goal feels impossible, or a sudden success is creating pressure to commit more. It is for situations in which a short delay is safe. When immediate safety, legal duty, medical urgency, or protection is involved, take the appropriate action rather than waiting for a workbook process.

The reset does not prohibit decisions. It prevents a temporary state from disguising itself as complete evidence.

The First Ten Minutes

Stop adding exposure. Do not send the irreversible message, transfer the money, sign the agreement, destroy the work, or promise a larger commitment while your range of attention is narrow.

Write five lines:

What happened: _______________________________________

What I feel in one or two words: _______________________

What I urgently want to do: ____________________________

What could become irreversible: ________________________

What must happen now for safety or duty: _______________

If nothing requires immediate action, protect a decision window. Tell relevant people when you will respond.

The First Two Hours

Regulate the body enough to think. Move to a safer or calmer setting if possible. Eat, hydrate, rest, breathe slowly, or contact a grounded person. Do not confuse compulsive research, repeated messaging, substance use, or rehearsing the conflict with regulation.

Then separate three columns:

Facts known now: _____________________________________

Interpretations and predictions: ______________________

Questions requiring evidence: _________________________

Do not debate the interpretations yet. Labeling them is enough.

The First Day

Return to the Goal Dossier and Decision History. What did you previously say would justify a change? Has that condition occurred? Is the current event part of a pattern or an exception?

Check four distortions:

Recency: Am I treating the latest event as the entire history?

Sunk cost: Am I trying to rescue what cannot be recovered?

Euphoria: Am I expanding commitment because one success makes limits feel unnecessary?

Identity threat: Am I trying to prove who I am rather than solve the actual problem?

Contact one person selected for relevance, not emotional intensity. Ask them to help you examine the decision, not simply confirm a direction.

The Second Day

Update the Evidence Ledger. Write the strongest case for continue, adjust, pause, and stop. Identify any override. Choose one of three outcomes:

Act now: Evidence is sufficient and delay adds cost.

Run a bounded test: A reversible action can reduce the key uncertainty.

Schedule a full decision meeting: Stakes or ambiguity require more preparation and participation.

Decision after reset: ____________________________________

Reason: _________________________________________________

New evidence that would change it: ________________________

Next review: ____________________________________________

The reset is not a rule that every difficult choice must wait forty-eight hours. Its discipline is proportionality. Create space when space is safe; act immediately when delay is the danger.

Workbook 17: Reengagement After an Ending

Stopping releases resources but does not automatically create direction. Reengagement is the deliberate movement toward another meaningful goal after a commitment has ended.

The next goal should not be selected only because it resembles the old one, repairs your public image, or removes the discomfort of empty space.

A. Complete the Release Inventory

What has been released?

Time per week: __________________________________________

Money or financial exposure: _____________________________

Attention and emotional load: ____________________________

Physical demand: ________________________________________

Social or organizational obligation: ______________________

Which resource needs recovery before reallocation? ________

Do not spend every released resource immediately. Recovery can be the first responsible allocation.

B. Harvest Without Forcing Meaning

List:

Assets that transfer: skills, relationships, credentials, tools, knowledge, reputation, or processes.

Lessons stored: a checklist, boundary, trigger, question, or skill plan.

Losses not redeemed: outcomes and costs that remain painful without needing to become secretly beneficial.

Obligations still open: anything that must be closed before full reengagement.

A lesson is not “Everything happens for a reason.” It is a specific change in future behavior.

C. Recover the Value

Return to the higher purpose. Which part remains alive after the method ends?

Value or need: ___________________________________________

How the old goal served it: ______________________________

How the old goal failed to serve it: ______________________

Other existing parts of life that serve it: _______________

Three possible new expressions:

_____________________________________________________

_____________________________________________________

_____________________________________________________

One possibility may be no immediate replacement. A person leaving an exhausting leadership role may need to recover before seeking another arena for contribution. A relationship ending may require grief rather than a rapid search for the next partner. A failed business may require stable employment before another venture.

D. Screen the New Goal

For each possible route, ask:

Do I want the daily practice or only the restored identity?

What evidence suggests a real need or opportunity?

Which capability transfers, and where am I a beginner?

What cost did I underestimate last time?

What will be different in the operating system?

Which people should be consulted before commitment?

What is the smallest reversible test?

What would make me decline even if the opportunity is exciting?

New route under consideration: ___________________________

Reason it deserves a test: _______________________________

Smallest responsible test: _______________________________

Maximum exposure: _______________________________________

Evidence required before deeper commitment: ______________

E. Protect Against the Rebound Goal

A rebound goal is selected mainly to reverse the feeling of the ending. It is often unusually public, urgent, or grand. The person wants a victory large enough to erase the last result.

Warning signs include:

The new commitment must be announced before it is tested.

The main attraction is proving doubters wrong.

Familiar risks are minimized because hesitation feels weak.

The goal promises to restore the exact identity that was lost.

Basic recovery, debt, or obligations are treated as distractions.

Feedback from cautious people creates disproportionate anger.

If these signs appear, reduce the scale and extend the observation period. A worthy new direction can survive responsible examination.

F. Create the Bridge Plan

Stability track: What protects income, housing, health, care duties, and routine?

________________________________________________________

Recovery track: What capacity must return?

________________________________________________________

Discovery track: What small tests explore possible routes?

________________________________________________________

Connection track: Who keeps you from becoming isolated or performing a false comeback?

________________________________________________________

Review point: When will you choose whether to deepen, extend, or close the exploration?

________________________________________________________

G. Make the New Commitment Smaller Than the New Insight

An ending can produce enormous clarity. Do not convert all of it into immediate obligation.

Commit to the next stage, not the entire imagined future. Enroll in the first prerequisite rather than declaring a new lifelong identity. Test the service before building the company around it. Volunteer in the setting before assuming the profession fits. Resume the practice before promising a public deadline.

Stage-one commitment: ___________________________________

Evidence for stage two: __________________________________

Turnaround rule: _________________________________________

Support conversation needed: _____________________________

Reengagement is not proof that stopping was correct. It is the responsible use of life after the stop. The new goal should be allowed to become itself rather than serving as an appeal against the old verdict.

Workbook 18: A Letter to the Future Decision-Maker

Long commitments change the person making them. Write this letter while you can still remember the conditions, hopes, and limits present at the beginning of the next period. Open it at the review date.

The letter creates continuity without demanding consistency. Its purpose is to help the future self distinguish new evidence from a rewritten history.

Begin with the date, place, and current direction.

Dear future decision-maker,

What I Am Choosing Now

Describe the goal and whether you are continuing, adjusting, pausing, stopping, or testing reengagement. State the decision in plain language. Do not write for an audience or future biography.

I am choosing to ________________________________________.

The period covered by this choice is _____________________.

Why the Decision Is Reasonable Now

Name the strongest evidence, not every encouraging fact. Include the most important contradictory evidence too.

The decision is supported by _____________________________.

The evidence that worries me most is _____________________.

I am proceeding despite that concern because ____________.

What I Expect

Write a forecast with a range. Include a result, cost, and emotional prediction.

By the review date, I expect _____________________________.

The best plausible result is _____________________________.

The difficult but plausible result is ____________________.

I expect the work to cost ________________________________.

I expect to feel ________________________________________.

Forecasting feelings matters because the future self may interpret expected discomfort as surprising evidence. If boredom, fear, grief, or uncertainty is part of the chosen cost, say so. This does not require tolerating harm.

What Must Be Protected

List the people, duties, resources, and values that the goal does not have permission to consume.

I will protect __________________________________________.

If __________________ occurs, the correct immediate action is __________________.

The person authorized to challenge me is ________________.

What I Am Likely to Forget

Write what history suggests you will minimize under pressure.

Perhaps you forget how quickly sleep loss changes judgment. Perhaps praise makes you expand too fast. Perhaps shame causes you to hide data. Perhaps proximity turns every warning into an obstacle to overcome.

When I am discouraged, I tend to forget _________________.

When I am excited, I tend to forget ______________________.

When other people are watching, I tend to _______________.

Please check whether that pattern is operating now.

What Would Justify Change

Give the future self permission to revise without inventing permission to drift.

Continue if _____________________________________________.

Adjust if ______________________________________________.

Pause if _______________________________________________.

Stop if ________________________________________________.

New evidence deserves more weight than my current preference when __________________.

What the Past Is Not Owed

Name the sunk cost that may demand repayment.

By the review date, I will have invested ________________.

That investment may create these real assets: ___________.

It will not be a reason by itself to _____________________.

What the Goal Means - and Does Not Mean

Protect identity from the outcome.

This goal expresses my values of ________________________.

It is not the only way to express them because __________.

Success would mean ______________________________________.

Failure or stopping would not mean _______________________.

The Request to the Future Self

End with instructions for the review.

Read the evidence before reading the story you have been telling.

Listen to ______________________________________________.

Acknowledge the cost carried by __________________________.

Do not make the decision merely to avoid feeling _________.

Choose the direction that best honors ____________________.

Whatever you choose, make the next action _______________.

Sign the letter. Place the review date on the calendar and store the letter where it will be found. If the decision is shared, consider exchanging letters or reading the relevant parts aloud.

When the date arrives, first record your current account without opening the letter. Then read it. Compare predictions, evidence, costs, and emotions. Notice where the earlier self was wise, afraid, naïve, or unable to see what later became obvious.

Do not obey the letter automatically. The earlier self did not possess the new evidence. Do not dismiss it automatically either. The earlier self may have been less invested and better able to name the boundary.

Write a response describing what changed and which direction you now choose. In this way, persistence becomes a conversation across time rather than a command issued once.

A Final Workbook Note

No record can make a difficult choice painless. The workbook cannot guarantee success, remove grief, equalize opportunity, or turn uncertain evidence into certainty.

It can slow the moment when one emotion tries to decide everything.

It can show whether effort is learning.

It can reveal whether the method still serves the reason.

It can give other people a truthful place in the decision.

It can preserve the words of the clearer self for the day when investment becomes loud.

Use it lightly enough to keep moving and seriously enough to be corrected.

Then choose the direction the evidence and your deepest responsibilities can defend.

About the Author

Sunday Pastores writes research-supported, story-driven books about human potential, reinvention, perseverance, and the decisions that shape a meaningful life. His work combines real-world case studies with practical exercises designed to move readers from insight to action.
